turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Come on in. I'll get you ready for Dr. Shah. What brings you in today?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): My stomach hurts, and I cannot sleep. Your parking garage is a maze, we went around twice.
[SEG0003] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'm Renata, I help her on weekdays. I drove.
[SEG0004] person_1 (NURSE): Glad you both made it. Blood pressure is one forty-eight over eighty-six.
[SEG0005] person_2 (PATIENT): My sister had hers checked at a church fair and acted like it was a crisis.
[SEG0006] person_1 (NURSE): Pulse is seventy-eight, oxygen is ninety-seven percent, temperature ninety-eight point two.
[SEG0007] person_1 (NURSE): Any allergies to medications?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): No. None. I can take whatever.
[SEG0009] person_3 (CAREGIVER): The ER said sulfa gave her a rash. I still have the paperwork at the apartment.
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): That was a wool sweater. A heat rash. I am not allergic to anything.
[SEG0011] person_3 (CAREGIVER): They wrote sulfa on the form. I'm not dropping it.
[SEG0012] person_1 (NURSE): I'll mark that as not settled. The doctor is on his way.
[SEG0013] person_4 (DOCTOR): Hello, I'm Dr. Shah. Stomach pain and poor sleep, that's the reason for the visit, yes?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes. Right under the ribs, a gnawing pain. And the nights are a mess.
[SEG0015] person_4 (DOCTOR): How long has the pain been going on?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Two weeks. No, sorry, a month. I couldn't finish the lemon pie at the bake sale, and that was a month ago.
[SEG0017] person_3 (CAREGIVER): It's been since before Easter. Three months, easy. She rubs her stomach all the time.
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): The Easter ham was separate. I overdid the ham, that's all.
[SEG0019] person_4 (DOCTOR): So about a month from you, about three months from Renata. I'll leave the start somewhere in that span, not nailed down.
[SEG0020] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any vomiting?
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I don't throw up.
[SEG0022] person_4 (DOCTOR): Nausea? That queasy feeling?
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Not queasy.
[SEG0024] person_4 (DOCTOR): What are your bowels doing? Any black stool, blood, or diarrhea?
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): The neighbor's beagle got into the trash Tuesday and barked till midnight. The whole street was up.
[SEG0026] person_4 (DOCTOR): That's a lot of dog. About the stool, though?
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): Normal. Brown, once a day. No blood, no diarrhea.
[SEG0028] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any fever or chills?
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): No fever and no chills.
[SEG0030] person_4 (DOCTOR): Chest pain, or shortness of breath?
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): No chest pain. I do get a little winded on the stairs, but that's the stairs, not my stomach.
[SEG0032] person_4 (DOCTOR): Does eating change the pain?
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): It gets worse after I eat. Spicy food, greasy food, or wine. Toast is okay.
[SEG0034] person_3 (CAREGIVER): And she still has two coffees every morning. That part is nonnegotiable.
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): My daughter in Phoenix says switch to tea. I am not moving to Phoenix, it's an oven down there.
[SEG0036] person_4 (DOCTOR): Is it heartburn, a burn that climbs into the chest?
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): I wouldn't call it heartburn. It stays put. It feels like a—
[SEG0038] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She stops talking and just holds her belly when it grabs her.
[SEG0039] person_4 (DOCTOR): Like a what?
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): Like a fist, right under the breastbone. A six out of ten when it's going.
[SEG0041] person_4 (DOCTOR): Tell me about the sleep.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): I wake up around two and the night is just over.
[SEG0043] person_4 (DOCTOR): When did that start?
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): Um, I can't put a date on it. Maybe sometime in the winter. I really don't know, it crept up.
[SEG0045] person_4 (DOCTOR): Have you lost weight?
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh, did you see that baking show, the one in the tent? Custard week, grown people crying over custard.
[SEG0047] person_4 (DOCTOR): I missed that one. The weight, though?
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): Pants fit the same. No weight loss.
[SEG0049] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Her appetite is off, though. She pushes the food around the plate.
[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): I do not. I eat fine. Don't tell him I'm not eating.
[SEG0051] person_4 (DOCTOR): You two don't agree on appetite, so I'll leave that unsettled. Any burning when you pee?
[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): No burning. I do get up to pee two, sometimes three times a night.
[SEG0053] person_4 (DOCTOR): What medicines are you on?
[SEG0054] person_2 (PATIENT): I almost left the bottle in the car, the parking got me so flustered. Blue cap.
[SEG0055] person_3 (CAREGIVER): That's the lisinopril. For her blood pressure.
[SEG0056] person_4 (DOCTOR): What dose?
[SEG0057] person_2 (PATIENT): Ten milligrams. No, scratch that, not ten, and not a hundred, that hundred was my sister's lab number. Twenty milligrams, once a day, by mouth, for the blood pressure.
[SEG0058] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She skips it some days. A couple of days a week, if she feels fine. I can't say she takes it the way it's written.
[SEG0059] person_2 (PATIENT): I take it most days. You're fussing.
[SEG0060] person_4 (DOCTOR): So the prescription is twenty milligrams daily, and whether every dose gets taken is still a bit up in the air. Anything else?
[SEG0061] person_2 (PATIENT): Advil, when my knees hurt. The two-hundred milligram tablets, two of them, a few times a week. Knees get stiff and achy.
[SEG0062] person_3 (CAREGIVER): And atorvastatin, forty milligrams every night, for her cholesterol.
[SEG0063] person_2 (PATIENT): Right, forty, every night. My last doctor started that.
[SEG0064] person_4 (DOCTOR): So the high blood pressure and the high cholesterol are ongoing. Any surgeries in the past?
[SEG0065] person_2 (PATIENT): Gallbladder came out about ten years ago. That's the only one.
[SEG0066] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any stomach problems in the family?
[SEG0067] person_2 (PATIENT): My mother had ulcers. They had her drinking milk for it, which sounds silly now.
[SEG0068] person_4 (DOCTOR): Do you smoke?
[SEG0069] person_2 (PATIENT): My dad smoked cigars in the house. The drapes held the smell for years after he passed.
[SEG0070] person_4 (DOCTOR): I meant you.
[SEG0071] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh. Never. I hated the smell.
[SEG0072] person_4 (DOCTOR): What about alcohol?
[SEG0073] person_2 (PATIENT): Socially.
[SEG0074] person_3 (CAREGIVER): It's a bottle of wine most nights.
[SEG0075] person_2 (PATIENT): Well, perhaps. Yes, a bottle, most nights, with dinner. It doesn't feel like a lot to me.
[SEG0076] person_4 (DOCTOR): Thank you, that's more useful than socially, and I'm not going to scold you. A bottle most nights can irritate the stomach and the liver, so I do want to check the liver.
[SEG0077] person_2 (PATIENT): If the next sentence is give up coffee, we are going to have words.
[SEG0078] person_4 (DOCTOR): No words, and I'm not making you quit coffee cold. Let me examine your belly.
[SEG0079] person_4 (DOCTOR): Abdomen is soft. It's tender when I press in the epigastrium, under the breastbone. No guarding and no rebound tenderness.
[SEG0080] person_2 (PATIENT): Ow, yes, that's the spot. And, well, actually, mornings I am queasy. Sick to my stomach until I eat a cracker. I told you I wasn't, but I am.

[SEG0081] person_4 (DOCTOR): I'm glad you came back to that. Thinking out loud, pain after meals, wine most nights, queasy in the morning, no vomiting, this fits gastritis best. I can't rule out an ulcer.
[SEG0082] person_2 (PATIENT): An ulcer sounds like my mother. I don't love that.

[SEG0083] person_4 (DOCTOR): It's on the list, not a settled diagnosis. I'm going to start omeprazole, forty, no, twenty milligrams is the better start, by mouth every morning, thirty minutes before breakfast, for the stomach pain.
[SEG0084] person_4 (DOCTOR): I'll also order liver blood tests, a hepatic panel, because of the wine and the pain. The lab can draw them today after we finish.
[SEG0085] person_2 (PATIENT): Needles. All right, I guess.

[SEG0086] person_4 (DOCTOR): Please stop the Advil while the stomach is irritated, it can make this worse. Ease off the spicy and greasy food, and try cutting the wine back. For sleep, no coffee after lunch, and keep a regular bedtime. If the pain turns severe, or you vomit blood, or you pass black stool, go to the ER.
[SEG0087] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'll put the Advil up high. The wine is going to be the argument.
[SEG0088] person_4 (DOCTOR): Come back in two weeks. We'll look at the liver tests and see if the omeprazole is helping. The front desk can book it.
[SEG0089] person_2 (PATIENT): Two weeks. If that beagle is quiet, maybe I'll have slept.
[SEG0090] person_4 (DOCTOR): We'll take the sleep as it comes. See you in two weeks.

spec.situation: Person attending for stomach pain and poor sleep; alcohol answered casually ('socially'), later 'a bottle of wine most nights, perhaps'; doctor non-judgemental; liver blood tests ordered; stomach medicine started.
features: self_correction: a speaker states a number, drug name or duration and then corrects it in the same turn or later ('seventy-five... no, hundred and fifty'). The label holds only the corrected value.
patient_answers_other_question: the patient answers a different question than the one asked, and the doctor repeats or lets it go.
interruptions_trailing_off: people interrupt each other, trail off, or the answer comes two turns after the question.

denial_then_admission: the patient first denies a symptom, then later describes it. The label records the symptom as present (the later, fuller answer) and does NOT also record the earlier denial as a negative finding.

bad.reason: Knees are stiff and achy, but frequency applies to Advil use, not clearly the symptom.
bad.text: stiff achy knees (category=musculoskeletal, status=present, severity=stiff and achy, frequency=a few times a week, temporality=current, body_site=knees, reported_by=patient, certainty=certain)

bad.reason: Patient takes 200 mg tablets, two at a time, a few times weekly; extracted dose should be 400 mg per use.
bad.text: Advil (generic_name=ibuprofen, dose=200 mg, frequency=2 tablets a few times a week, indication=knee pain, status=currently_used, reported_by=patient)

omissions.text: Black stool/melena was specifically asked about and denied ('No blood, no diarrhea' plus 'Normal. Brown, once a day'); only blood in stool and diarrhea were recorded, not the denial of black stool.
Bowel habits were described as normal brown stool once daily.

Nausea was initially denied when asked ('No. Not queasy.') and later corrected to present as morning queasiness relieved by a cracker; the explicit earlier denial/conflict was not recorded as an uncertainty.
Epigastric pain was described as staying put under the breastbone rather than climbing into the chest; this supports the denial of heartburn/reflux-type radiation.
Alcohol history was initially given as 'socially' before being clarified to a bottle of wine most nights; this disagreement/correction was not recorded as a clinical uncertainty.
Atorvastatin was confirmed by the patient as 'forty, every night' after caregiver initially named it; recorded only as reported by caregiver.
The planned follow-up purpose was to review the liver tests and assess whether omeprazole is helping.
